newsitem.title: USA: U.S. expected to join international Zaire force.
newsitem.headline: U.S. expected to join international Zaire force.

text.p: After days of hesitation, the United States was expected to announce on Wednesday it will take part in an international force to intervene in Zaire's humanitarian crisis, U.S. officials said.

"That is currently under very extensive discussion at the highest levels of government today and I think an announcement will shortly be made about our intention to join the international force," Undersecretary of State for Global Affairs Tim Wirth said at a World Food Summit in Rome.

Speaking to reporters, Wirth also praised an offer by Canada to command such a force to help bring assistance to over one million starving Hutu refugees caught in the crossfire of four weeks of fighting.
An adminstration official in Washington said: "We will be contributing troops to some sort of force."
Diplomats at the United Nations said they expected the United States, and later Britain, to announce plans to join the international force.
This would clear the way for the U.N. Security Council to get to work on a resolution, which Canada has already drafted, that could be adopted before the end of the week.
Many details remain to be firmed up and the initial U.S. announcement would be a tentative commitment to participate, not a final decision, said one U.S. official.

Officials said the U.S. role is expected to involve about 3,000 American troops who would provide logistics support and secure the airport at Goma in eastern Zaire in order to get humanitarian relief supplies to more than one million refugees said to be at risk.

The officials said they expected about 12 countries to take part in the force but it was uncertain when the relief operation might begin. A U.S. military team was in Uganda on Wednesday, trying to get to neighbouring Zaire to assess the situation. It was unknown when the team might report to Washington.
The United States has been under mounting pressure to join in the multinational effort, especially from France and Canada, which has offered to lead the military force.

But despite an apparent consensus that the Zaire crisis could lead to thousands of deaths without urgent international action, President Bill Clinton -- re-elected last week to a second term -- and other senior officials have approached the matter with great reluctance and caution.
The United States has painful memories of a U.N. relief mission to Somalia in 1993 which led to heavy casualties among U.S. and other troops.

The adminstration is concerned that the mission of any military intervention force in Zaire be clearly defined, with a clear target for withdrawing troops. Bosnia, where the NATO-led implementation force called IFOR is helping enforce a detailed peace agreement, is seen as the example to follow.
Clinton discussed Zaire's refugee crisis with other world leaders by telephone on Wednesday and a White House announcement was expected later, officials said.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said that among those consulted would be Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien.

A delegation of senior Canadian officials met senior U.S. officials at the White House on Tuesday, including Lieutenant-General Joseph Maurice Baril, the former chief U.N. military adviser, who has been named to head the Zaire force.
Diplomatic sources said Canada wanted an operation of more than 10,000 troops and has promised to supply 1,500 itself.
The mission of the proposed force would be to aid starving refugees in eastern Zaire who have been fleeing fighting between Tutsi rebels and Zaire's army.

McCurry said that before committing U.S. troops, Clinton wanted to reconcile "different objectives and different ideas presented by different nations" and seek the support of African countries whose interests might be affected.

"Even facing an urgent humanitarian situation, there always is a necessity for the commander-in-chief to have a very clear focus on mission priorities, objectives, who participates, how the force would be structured, what the nature and the duration of the mission would be, and how do you measure success and how do you get out," McCurry said.
